---
title: "Exercises — Chromatin and protein–DNA"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution**. The reasoning is the point, not the answer.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
open for the enzyme question, and the protocol pages on
[NGS 101](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/) for the comparisons.

# Part 1 — What the reads mean

## E1. One read, one sentence

For each method, complete the sentence "one read is ...": ATAC-seq, MNase-seq, ChIP-seq,
CUT&RUN, DamID. Then say which of the five gives you a signal that is **not** the end of a
DNA fragment the enzyme made.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask for each method what happened to the DNA that is now at the start of the read, and what
did that.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- ATAC-seq: a Tn5 insertion point, so a base that was accessible.
- MNase-seq: the edge of a stretch of DNA that a nucleosome protected from the nuclease.
- ChIP-seq: the end of a sonicated fragment that carried the protein. The site is somewhere
  inside the fragment, not at the read start.
- CUT&RUN: the edge of DNA protected by the bound protein, where MNase was stopped.
- DamID: a GATC site that was methylated on adenine, then cut by DpnI.

DamID is the odd one out. The read start is a GATC cut by DpnI, but the information is the
**methylation mark** the fusion protein wrote earlier. It reports where the protein had been,
not where an enzyme cut because of it.
:::

## E2. A ladder that is missing

An ATAC-seq library from 50,000 human cells gives a fragment-size trace with one tall peak
below 100 bp and no peaks at about 200 and 400 bp. What are two possible explanations, and
which change to the protocol would you try first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The ladder exists because Tn5 cuts only occasionally between nucleosomes. What would make it
cut everywhere, and what would remove the nucleosomes?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. **Over-transposition.** Too much Tn5 for the number of nuclei, for example because the
   cells were counted wrongly or many were lost. Tn5 cuts every accessible stretch many times
   and also reaches into more nucleosome-wrapped DNA, so only short pieces remain. Fix: count
   nuclei carefully, scale the enzyme to the cell number, and shorten the reaction.
2. **Damaged or lysed nuclei.** If the chromatin has been stripped or degraded, there is no
   nucleosome pattern to protect the DNA, and Tn5 acts on naked DNA. Fix: gentler lysis, fresh
   cells, avoid freeze-thaw of the cell pellet.

Try the first: it is the cheapest change, and the other cause would also show as low viability
before you start.
:::

## E3. Where the reads go

A cell has about 6.2 billion bp of nuclear DNA (diploid). Suppose 3% of it is accessible to
Tn5, and that Tn5 inserts equally often per base in every accessible region, including
mitochondrial DNA. The mitochondrial genome is 16.6 kb long and fully accessible.

What fraction of reads would be mitochondrial in a cell with 1,000 copies of mtDNA, and in
one with 5,000? What does this tell you about Omni-ATAC's extra wash?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Compare the **accessible base pairs** from the two sources. Nuclear accessible DNA is 3% of
6.2 Gb.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Accessible nuclear DNA: 0.03 × 6.2 × 10⁹ ≈ 186 Mb.

- 1,000 copies: 16.6 kb × 1,000 = 16.6 Mb; fraction = 16.6 / (186 + 16.6) ≈ **8%**.
- 5,000 copies: 83 Mb; fraction = 83 / (186 + 83) ≈ **31%**.

The assumptions are illustrative: copy number differs between cell types, and the nuclear
share of accessible DNA is not exactly 3%. The point is that mitochondrial DNA has no
nucleosomes, so it takes a large share of reads in cells with many copies. Omni-ATAC washes
with detergent-containing buffer before transposition, so mitochondria released by lysis are
removed rather than carried into the reaction.
:::

# Part 2 — Design problems

## E4. Choose the enzyme

You want to profile a transcription factor from 10,000 human cells. You have a good rabbit
antibody. Compare pA-MNase and pA-Tn5 as the tethered enzyme. State which property of each
decides the choice, and which you would use for a first attempt.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Look at the NEB charts for what each enzyme leaves at the ends. Then think about what the
washes do to a protein that binds DNA weakly and briefly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- **pA-MNase** (CUT&RUN): works in physiological salt, so weakly bound factors stay. It
  releases short fragments that mirror the protein's footprint. The cost is a library step
  after extraction.
- **pA-Tn5** (CUT&Tag): the library is made in the same reaction, so it is more economical at
  low input. The usual high-salt washes remove Tn5 that is bound non-specifically, but they can
  also remove a weakly bound transcription factor. Tn5 also prefers open DNA, which creates
  background at accessible sites.

For a first attempt on a transcription factor I would choose CUT&RUN: it is the better
established method for TFs, and the salt conditions are gentler. For histone marks, CUT&Tag.
Both need an IgG control.
:::

## E5. The control that is missing

You ChIP an unrelated factor and get strong peaks at the promoters of highly expressed genes.
A colleague says the factor is a general activator. What is your alternative explanation, and
what two controls would settle it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Remember what sonication does to open versus closed chromatin.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Open chromatin shears more easily and is over-represented in the input of any ChIP, and
highly expressed loci can be pulled down non-specifically. The peaks may reflect the
chromatin, not the factor.

Controls: (1) a **sequenced input** (sonicated, no antibody) to see the baseline at those
promoters, and (2) an **IgG or knock-out/knock-down control** to see what the antibody pulls
down without its target. Biological replicates, and a second antibody if available, add
further confidence.
:::

## E6. Footprints

You want to ask whether a transcription factor occupies its motif in ATAC-seq data from one
human cell type. List what you need in the data and in the analysis for a footprint to be
believable.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A footprint is a few tens of bases. How many insertions fall there? And what else could make a
dip?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- **Depth**: a footprint is a dip in the number of insertions over a few tens of bases, so you
  need many insertions aggregated over many sites of the same motif.
- **Insertion positions**, not fragments or read centres, shifted for the Tn5 offset.
- **Bias correction**: Tn5 has a sequence preference, so a dip can be a sequence effect. Compare
  with Tn5 on naked genomic DNA, or use a model of the cutting bias.
- **Orthogonal evidence**: a ChIP or CUT&RUN profile of the same factor.

Bulk accessibility data do not show which of two alleles or cells carried the factor.
:::

## E7. The step that restores the molecule

After tagmentation, the DNA is purified and the PCR begins with 5 minutes at 72 °C before the
first denaturation. Why? What happens if you leave it out, and will you get an error message?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Tn5 transfers one strand of each adapter. What does the other strand look like at the 9 nt gap?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Tn5 joins one strand of each adapter to the 5' end of the fragment; the other strand is left
with a 9 nt gap. During the 72 °C step the polymerase extends the 3' end of the fragment's
other strand across the gap, copying the adapter sequence, so that both strands become full
templates for the primers.

Without it the first cycles are much less efficient and the library is poor in yield. There
is no error message: the PCR runs, and the result is a weak or absent library.
:::

## E8. Count the marks

DamID depends on GATC sites. In a random genome of 3.1 Gb, how many GATC sites do you expect,
and what is the average spacing? What does this imply for resolution, and why must a Dam-only
control be run?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
A 4 bp site appears once per 4⁴ bases in random sequence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
4⁴ = 256, so one site per 256 bp on average: 3.1 × 10⁹ / 256 ≈ **12 million** sites. The real
number differs because the genome is not random.

The average spacing is a few hundred bp, but the methylation from a tethered Dam extends
beyond one site, and the reads are placed at the fragments between GATC sites. As a result
resolution is in the range of kilobases rather than base pairs.

A free Dam methylates open, accessible DNA on its own, so without a Dam-only control you would
mistake accessibility for binding.
:::

## E9. A reversal that was forgotten

A student performs ChIP-seq but accidentally skips the overnight 65 °C step. They still
proceed with proteinase K and column purification. What do they see, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which bonds does the heat break, and what does proteinase K do on its own?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Formaldehyde crosslinks are reversed by heat, not by protease. Proteinase K digests the
protein, but peptide remnants stay covalently attached to the DNA. Such DNA tends to be lost
in the purification and to inhibit the enzymes of library construction, so the yield is very
low. The loss falls on the immunoprecipitated DNA, since that is the DNA with protein attached.
You would see an empty or failed ChIP library, with no error message to explain it.
:::

# Self-check

Answer without looking anything up.

1. What is the difference between "cut and keep" and "pull down" methods?
2. Why does ATAC-seq need paired-end reads to show a nucleosome ladder?
3. What does protein A do in pA-MNase?
4. Why does CUT&RUN have lower background than ChIP?
5. What is the 72 °C step in ATAC and CUT&Tag libraries for?
6. What does a calling-card read represent?
7. Which two controls does every ChIP-like experiment need?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. In cut and keep, the enzyme cuts and the cut ends are the library (DNase, ATAC, MNase).
   In pull down, the DNA is cut everywhere and an antibody selects (ChIP, DAP-seq).
2. The ladder is in the fragment **length**, which needs both ends of each fragment.
3. It binds the constant region of the antibody, bringing the enzyme to the target.
4. Only the DNA released at the target leaves the nucleus; the rest is never in solution.
5. It fills the gap left by Tn5, so the adapter sequence can be copied.
6. A transposon insertion site, left near where the TF was bound while it was expressed.
7. A sequenced input or IgG control for background, and replicates.
:::

# Going further

- Open the [Omni-ATAC](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/omni-atac__10.1038+nmeth.4396/omni-atac.html)
  and [CUT&Tag](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/cut-tag__10.1038+s41467-019-09982-5/cut-tag.html)
  pages. Both end in the same Tn5 library. Write down, step by step, where the adapters come
  from and which steps could be skipped in each.
- Take a published track of a histone mark and ask, before looking at the methods, which of the
  methods in this unit made it. What features would give it away?
